questions.q: A phone app shows your list of tasks. Where does the backend fit in?
questions.explain: The tasks are not stored on the phone. The app asks another computer for them, and a program there answers. That program is the backend. The screen you see is the front end.
options: It is the screen of the app that shows the tasks
It is a program on another computer that stores the tasks and answers the app
It is the part of the phone that saves files
It is the app store the app was downloaded from

questions.q: In which order does the course teach its four tools?
questions.explain: You start with the language (JavaScript), then the program that runs it on a server (Node.js), then types (TypeScript), and finally the framework (ZudoJS).
options: JavaScript, Node.js, TypeScript, ZudoJS
ZudoJS, TypeScript, Node.js, JavaScript
TypeScript, JavaScript, ZudoJS, Node.js
Node.js, ZudoJS, JavaScript, TypeScript

questions.q: What is Node.js?
questions.explain: Node.js is not a new language. It is a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, for example on a server. The set of ready-made parts is ZudoJS, the framework.
options: A second programming language that replaces JavaScript
The program that runs JavaScript on a server
A website where you download JavaScript code
A framework made of ready-made backend parts

questions.q: What does TypeScript add to JavaScript?
questions.explain: TypeScript is JavaScript with types. The types let tools find many mistakes before you run the program, instead of when a user hits them.
options: A faster way to run code in the browser
A database for storing your data
Types, which catch many mistakes before the code runs
A terminal for typing commands

questions.q: The lesson calls ZudoJS a framework. What is a framework?
questions.explain: A framework gives you ready-made parts, so you do not write everything from zero. ZudoJS is a framework for building backends in TypeScript.
options: A set of ready-made parts for building applications, such as backends
A programming language that runs only on servers
A program that edits code files
A list of lessons to follow in order

questions.q: Why does the course teach backends without a framework first, before ZudoJS?
questions.explain: ZudoJS is the destination, not the starting point. If you have built the pieces by hand first, the framework is no longer magic: you understand the problems it solves.
options: Because ZudoJS only works after you finish every lesson
So that when you meet ZudoJS, you know exactly what each part does for you
Because frameworks are not used in real jobs
Because ZudoJS cannot run JavaScript code

questions.q: You have never written code. How should you use this course?
questions.explain: Complete beginners follow every lesson in order. Each new word is explained the first time it appears, so skipping ahead means missing those explanations.
options: Start at Meet ZudoJS, because that is the goal
Skip JavaScript and start with TypeScript
Start at the beginning and follow every lesson in order
Read only the Recap of each lesson

questions.q: You already know Python. What does the lesson advise about the first JavaScript lessons?
questions.explain: Knowing another language helps, so the start feels quick. But JavaScript has its own rules and surprises, so the lesson tells you to read those parts anyway.
options: They will feel quick, but read them anyway, because JavaScript has its own surprises
Skip them, because every language works the same way
Start at the Production part instead
Learn Python again first, then come back

questions.q: What do you need to take this course?
questions.explain: You only need a computer where you can install programs, on Windows, macOS or Linux. You do not need to be good at maths, and the course is free.
options: A paid account and a fast server
Good maths skills and a Mac
An existing project written in JavaScript
A computer with Windows, macOS or Linux where you can install programs

questions.q: Which three projects do you build in this course, from smallest to biggest?
questions.explain: Each project is bigger than the last: the Task API first, then the BookStore API in TypeScript, then ShopFlow, the capstone in the Production part.
options: ShopFlow, BookStore API, Task API
Task API, BookStore API, ShopFlow
BookStore API, Task API, ShopFlow
Task API, ShopFlow, BookStore API

questions.q: What is the Task API?
questions.explain: The Task API stores tasks. You write it first with plain Node.js, then rebuild it with ZudoJS. The book shop is the BookStore API, and the commerce backend is ShopFlow.
options: A backend that stores tasks and lets people create, list, update and complete them
A small shop for books written in TypeScript
A phone app that shows a to-do list
A complete commerce backend with orders and products

questions.q: The BookStore API is written in TypeScript with no framework. Why?
questions.explain: Building it by hand shows you the repeated work and problems that a framework removes. The final project is ShopFlow, not the BookStore API.
options: Because ZudoJS cannot sell books
Because TypeScript projects must never use a framework
To show you the problems a framework exists to solve
Because it is the final project of the course

questions.q: What is ShopFlow?
questions.explain: ShopFlow is the capstone in the Production part: products, orders, users and background work, ready to deploy. A capstone is the big final project that uses everything you learned.
options: The first project, written in plain JavaScript
The name of the browser terminal on each page
A tool that marks lessons as done
The capstone: a complete commerce backend prepared for deployment

questions.q: How is the Task API written during the course?
questions.explain: You write the Task API by hand with Node.js first. Later you rebuild it with ZudoJS and add a database, users, permissions, events, queues and tests.
options: Only once, with ZudoJS from the start
First with plain Node.js, then rebuilt with ZudoJS, adding a database, users and more
First in Python, then in JavaScript
Only in the browser terminal, never on your computer

questions.q: Which of these is not on the lesson's list of things you will know by the end?
questions.explain: The course is about backends: JavaScript, Node.js, HTTP, databases, TypeScript, ZudoJS and production work such as Docker. Building phone apps is not part of it.
options: Databases and SQL with PostgreSQL
Deployment with Docker
Building phone apps with a mobile toolkit
Where types stop and runtime checks must begin

questions.q: The lesson says you will learn "where types stop and runtime checks must begin". What does that point to?
questions.explain: Types catch mistakes before the code runs. But data from users or other programs arrives while it runs, and types cannot check that. So a backend must also check data at run time.
options: Types make runtime checks useless, so you never need them
TypeScript types help while you write code, but data arriving while the program runs must still be checked
Runtime checks are only needed in the browser
Types and runtime checks are two names for the same thing

questions.q: How is the course organised?
questions.explain: There are 84 lessons in 17 parts. A part is a group of lessons on one subject, like "JavaScript fundamentals" or "Data".
options: 84 parts, each with one lesson
17 lessons in 84 parts
84 lessons grouped into 17 parts
4 lessons, one for each tool

questions.q: What is a part in this course?
questions.explain: A part groups lessons on one subject. The label that says how much you need something is the tier, not the part.
options: A group of lessons on one subject
One section inside a lesson
A label that says how much you need a lesson
A project you build

questions.q: What does the Foundation tier mean?
questions.explain: Foundation parts (Start here, JavaScript, Node.js and npm, Backend fundamentals, TypeScript) must be understood before you continue. "Required for everyday ZudoJS work" is Core.
options: Learn it when you prepare a real application for deployment
Learn it when your application needs it
Required for everyday ZudoJS work
You must understand it before moving on

questions.q: The "Events and background work" part is Advanced. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: Advanced means "learn it when your application needs it". It is not forbidden for beginners; it is just not required before you move on.
options: You must finish it before any other part
Learn it when your application needs it
It is only for experts, so beginners should never read it
It is required for every ZudoJS project

questions.q: When should you learn the Production tier?
questions.explain: The Production tier covers what you need to deploy and run a real system. You learn it when you prepare an application for deployment.
options: Before you write your first line of JavaScript
Never, it is optional reading only
When you prepare a real application for deployment
Right after the Welcome lesson

questions.q: Kemi already builds websites with JavaScript in the browser but has never written a server. Where should Kemi start?
questions.explain: People who already know JavaScript can skip the JavaScript part. How the web works is worth reading if the web is new, then Node.js and npm is the next step.
options: At the very first JavaScript lesson, with no skipping
Read How the web works to be sure, then start at Node.js and npm
At Meet ZudoJS
At the Production part

questions.q: Lee writes TypeScript backends every day. Where should Lee start?
questions.explain: Someone who knows TypeScript and backends goes straight to Meet ZudoJS. If a lesson uses something skipped, it links back to the lesson that teaches it.
options: At Your developer environment
At the JavaScript values lesson
At How programs run
At Meet ZudoJS, following links back when something is new

questions.q: What comes at the end of every lesson page?
questions.explain: Each lesson has short sections with an example and its output, then a Practice section with exercises and a Recap of the main points.
options: A list of all 84 lessons
A Practice section with exercises, and a Recap
A video of the whole lesson
A form to create an account

questions.q: You press Run in browser under an example. What happens?
questions.explain: The browser terminal opens at the bottom of the page and runs the example right there. You can change the code and run it again with Run or Ctrl + Enter.
options: The code is sent to your computer's terminal
The code is saved to a file on your computer
A terminal opens at the bottom of the page and runs the code
The page downloads Node.js for you

questions.q: An example is marked Node.js only. Why can it not run in the browser?
questions.explain: Browsers are not allowed to read your files or start web servers. Examples that do that must run on your own computer with Node.js.
options: Because it has a mistake in it
It uses things a browser cannot do, like reading files or starting a web server
Because it prints more than two lines
Because the browser terminal only runs TypeScript

questions.q: A box shows $ node --version. What do you type in your terminal?
questions.explain: A line starting with $ is a command for you to type, but you do not type the $ itself. The lines under it (like v24.19.0) are what the computer printed back.
options: $ node --version
node --version
$node--version
v24.19.0

questions.q: In a command box, what are the lines without a $ in front?
questions.explain: Only lines that start with $ are commands. The lines under a command are its output, for example the version number that node --version prints.
options: More commands you must type
Comments you can ignore
What the computer printed back after the command
Error messages that mean the command failed

questions.q: Your computer prints something different from the output shown in a lesson. What is the most likely reason?
questions.explain: Every output on the pages is real: it was produced by running the code. So a difference usually means a small typing mistake, and finding it is part of learning.
options: The output on the page was typed by hand and is often wrong
A small typing mistake in your code, so compare carefully
Your computer is broken
JavaScript prints random results

questions.q: Where is your "Mark this lesson as done" progress saved?
questions.explain: Progress is saved in your browser on this device. You do not need an account. On another computer or browser, your ticks are not there.
options: In your account on the course server
In a file in your project folder
In your browser, on this device only
It is not saved at all

questions.q: You are afraid to change the code in the browser terminal. What does the lesson say?
questions.explain: The browser terminal is a safe place to try things. Change the code, press Run, and see what happens.
options: Change it only after making a backup of your computer
Changes are sent to all other learners
Nothing you type there can break anything, so experiment freely
You can only run the code once

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each console.log prints one line. The quotes are not printed. When you give it two values separated by a comma, it prints them with one space between them.
questions.code:
console.log("Hello! I am learning backend development.");
console.log("Lessons in this course:", 84);
options:
Hello! I am learning backend development.
Lessons in this course: 84
Hello! I am learning backend development. Lessons in this course: 84

"Hello! I am learning backend development."
"Lessons in this course:", 84

Hello! I am learning backend development.
Lessons in this course:84

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The program runs from top to bottom, one line at a time. Each console.log prints its own line, in the order the lines are written.
options:
first
second
third

third
second
first
first second third

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The quotes only mark where the text starts and ends. console.log prints the text inside them, without the quotes.
questions.code: console.log("I want to build an API.");
options: I want to build an API.
"I want to build an API."
console.log("I want to build an API.")

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: console.log prints every value you give it on one line, with a single space between them. The commas in the code separate the values; they are not printed.
options: Parts: 17 Lessons: 84
Parts:17Lessons:84
Parts:, 17, Lessons:, 84
Parts: 17, Lessons: 84

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first line prints the number 84, the second prints the text "84". On their own, both look the same: console.log does not show the quotes of a string.

questions.q: Ada changed the example and ran it. What does it print?
questions.explain: Two console.log calls print two lines, each exactly as written between the quotes.
questions.code:
console.log("My name is Ada.");
console.log("I want to build an API for my to-do list.");
options:
My name is Ada.
I want to build an API for my to-do list.
My name is Ada. I want to build an API for my to-do list.
My name is Ada.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call prints one line, top to bottom. The two values in each call are joined with one space.
options:
Tier: Foundation
Tier: Core
Tier: Foundation Tier: Core

Tier:Foundation
Tier:Core

Tier: Core
Tier: Foundation

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Text is printed exactly as written, including upper- and lower-case letters. The computer does not "fix" your spelling.
options:
ZudoJS
zudojs

ZudoJS
ZudoJS

zudojs
zudojs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A comma gives console.log two values, which it prints with a space between them. + joins two texts into one, with no space added.
options:
Task API
TaskAPI

Task API
Task API

TaskAPI
TaskAPI

Task, API
TaskAPI

questions.q: Lesson pages live under /learn/. What does this print?
questions.explain: + between two texts glues them together exactly, with no space and nothing removed. So you get the path /learn/setup.
options: /learn/setup
/learn/ setup
"/learn/" + "setup"
/learn//setup

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Numbers without quotes are real numbers, so 1 + 1 + 1 is calculated first and gives 3. Only text inside quotes is printed as written.
options: Projects: 3
Projects: 1 + 1 + 1
Projects: 111

questions.q: Write one line of code that prints exactly Hello, ZudoJS!
questions.explain: Put the text in quotes inside console.log( ). It prints the text without the quotes: console.log("Hello, ZudoJS!");.

questions.q: Print two lines: first I start with JavaScript., then I finish with ZudoJS.
questions.explain: Use one console.log per line. The program runs from top to bottom, so write them in the order you want them printed.
questions.starter:
// line 1: I start with JavaScript.
// line 2: I finish with ZudoJS.
questions.expected:
I start with JavaScript.
I finish with ZudoJS.
questions.solution:
console.log("I start with JavaScript.");
console.log("I finish with ZudoJS.");

questions.q: Use one console.log with two values (a text and a number) to print Projects to build: 3
questions.explain: Separate the two values with a comma: console.log("Projects to build:", 3);. console.log adds one space between them.

questions.q: Print the four tools of the course, one per line, in the order the course teaches them: JavaScript, Node.js, TypeScript, ZudoJS.
questions.explain: Four console.log calls give four lines, top to bottom: the language, the program that runs it on a server, types, then the framework.
questions.starter: // print the four tools, one per line

questions.q: This program prints the three projects in the wrong order. Fix it so it prints Task API, BookStore API, ShopFlow, one per line, from smallest to biggest.
questions.explain: Lines run from top to bottom, so the order of the lines is the order of the output. Move the lines so the Task API comes first and ShopFlow last.

questions.q: Lesson pages are at /learn/ followed by the lesson name. Use + to join "/learn/" and "welcome", and print the result: /learn/welcome
questions.explain: + between two texts joins them exactly: "/learn/" + "welcome" is "/learn/welcome".
questions.starter: // join "/learn/" and "welcome" with +, then print it
